name: Simple moving average
definition: The unweighted arithmetic mean of the last n observations (usually closing prices), recomputed each period as the window slides forward; the most basic trend-following overlay.
intuition: A rolling average that smooths day-to-day noise so the underlying trend is easier to see. Every observation in the window counts equally.
mechanics: Sum the last n prices and divide by n; each new bar drops the oldest point and adds the newest, so the average moves through time. Used to define trend direction, support/resistance zones, and as a building block for other indicators such as Bollinger Bands and MACD.
formula: SMA(n) = (P_1 + P_2 + ... + P_n) / n, where P_i are the last n prices (usually closes) and n is the window length.
failure_modes: It is a lagging, trend-following measure: the longer the window the greater the lag, and in sideways, trendless markets price crosses it repeatedly, producing whipsaws.
misconceptions: A moving average does not predict future prices; it defines the current trend from past data. Nor is any single length (e.g. the 200-day) inherently significant beyond convention and self-reinforcing usage.
example: Closes of 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 give a 5-day SMA of 13; when the next close is 16, the SMA becomes (12+13+14+15+16)/5 = 14.

name: Exponential moving average
definition: A recursively computed moving average whose weights decay geometrically with age, giving recent observations more influence and reducing lag relative to a same-length simple moving average.
intuition: Like a simple average, but today's price counts more than last week's, so it reacts faster to new information.
mechanics: EMA_t = k*P_t + (1-k)*EMA_{t-1} with k = 2/(n+1), seeded with an SMA. Because each value depends on all previous values, a long history (hundreds of bars) is needed for the series to converge to accurate values.
formula: EMA_t = k * P_t + (1 - k) * EMA_{t-1}; k = 2/(n+1); P_t = current price; n = period.
failure_modes: Still a lagging trend-follower: less lag than an SMA means more sensitivity to noise, so it whipsaws sooner and more often in trading ranges.
misconceptions: An EMA is not inherently better than an SMA — it trades lag for noise sensitivity. Also, early EMA values depend on the seed, so short data histories yield inaccurate values.
example: A 10-day EMA applies an 18.18% weight (2/11) to the latest close; a 20-day EMA applies 9.52% (2/21).

name: Weighted moving average
definition: A moving average that weights observations linearly by recency — the newest price gets weight n, the next n-1, down to 1 — so recent data dominates while the window length stays fixed.
intuition: A compromise between the SMA and EMA: recent prices matter more, but the weights decline in a straight line rather than exponentially.
mechanics: Multiply each of the last n prices by its recency rank, sum the products, and divide by the sum of the weights n(n+1)/2. Recomputed fresh each bar; not recursive.
formula: WMA(n) = sum(i * P_i, i=1..n) / sum(i, i=1..n), with P_n the most recent price; the denominator equals n(n+1)/2.
failure_modes: Lags like all averages and whipsaws in ranges; the abrupt weight cutoff at the window edge makes it twitchy when a large old value exits the window.
misconceptions: A WMA is not an EMA: WMA weights decline linearly over a fixed window, whereas EMA weights decay exponentially over an effectively infinite history.
example: With closes 10, 11, 12, the 3-period WMA = (1*10 + 2*11 + 3*12)/6 = 68/6 = 11.33, versus an SMA of 11.

name: Smoothed moving average
definition: A recursive moving average (also called modified or running moving average) equivalent to an EMA with smoothing constant 1/n, so it smooths far more heavily than a same-length standard EMA.
intuition: The gentlest common average: each new price is absorbed at only 1/n weight, so the line moves slowly and filters a great deal of noise.
mechanics: Seeded with an n-period SMA; thereafter SMMA_t = (SMMA_{t-1}*(n-1) + P_t)/n. This is the smoothing Welles Wilder used for RSI, ATR, and ADX, and the average used in Bill Williams' Alligator lines.
formula: SMMA_t = (SMMA_{t-1} * (n - 1) + P_t) / n; first value = SMA of the first n prices.
failure_modes: Very heavy lag; early values depend strongly on the seed and need long histories to stabilize, so short data sets give unreliable readings.
misconceptions: SMMA(n) is not the same as EMA(n): its alpha is 1/n rather than 2/(n+1), so a 14-period SMMA responds roughly like a 27-period standard EMA.
example: If the prior 14-period SMMA is 50 and the new close is 52, SMMA = (50*13 + 52)/14 = 50.14.

name: Hull moving average
definition: Alan Hull's moving average (2005), engineered to nearly eliminate lag while retaining smoothness by combining weighted moving averages of different lengths with a lag-canceling correction term.
intuition: An average designed to hug price closely without becoming jagged — fast like a short WMA, smooth like a long one.
mechanics: Compute WMA(n/2) and WMA(n) of price, form the raw series 2*WMA(n/2) - WMA(n) to cancel lag, then smooth the result with a WMA of length sqrt(n), rounding non-integer periods to whole numbers.
formula: HMA(n) = WMA( 2*WMA(P, n/2) - WMA(P, n), sqrt(n) ), where WMA(P, m) is the m-period weighted moving average of price.
failure_modes: Reduced lag means reduced noise filtering: it whipsaws in sideways markets and remains a trend-follower, not a predictor.
misconceptions: Hull himself advises against HMA crossover systems — crossovers exploit lag differences that the HMA was built to remove; use turns in the HMA's direction instead.
example: For an 11-period HMA, use WMA(6) and WMA(11) for the raw line, then smooth with a 3-period WMA (sqrt(11) = 3.3 rounds to 3).

name: Triangular moving average
definition: A double-smoothed simple moving average — an SMA of an SMA — whose effective weights form a triangle that peaks at the middle of the window, giving mid-window data the most influence.
intuition: Averaging an average: extra smooth at the cost of extra lag, with the middle of the window weighted most.
mechanics: TMA(n) = SMA( SMA(P, m1), m2 ) with m1 = ceil((n+1)/2) and m2 = floor((n+1)/2); equivalently a single convolution with triangular weights 1, 2, ..., m, ..., 2, 1.
formula: TMA(n) = SMA( SMA(P, ceil((n+1)/2)), floor((n+1)/2) ).
failure_modes: Twice the smoothing means roughly twice the lag of its component SMA, so it is poor for timing and usable mainly as a slow trend reference.
misconceptions: Despite the peaked weighting it is not centered in the signal sense — it uses past data only and still lags; a true centered moving average uses future data and cannot be computed in real time.
example: A 5-period TMA = SMA(SMA(P, 3), 3); if the last three 3-period SMA values are 10, 11, 12, the TMA is 11.

name: Variable index dynamic average
definition: Tushar Chande's Variable Index Dynamic Average: an exponential-style moving average whose smoothing constant is scaled each bar by a volatility index — the absolute Chande Momentum Oscillator — so it reacts faster in decisive, volatile markets and slower in quiet ones.
intuition: An adaptive average that automatically speeds up when the market is moving decisively and slows down when it is drifting.
mechanics: VIDYA_t = VIDYA_{t-1} + alpha * |CMO_t|/100 * (P_t - VIDYA_{t-1}), with alpha = 2/(n+1). When |CMO| nears 100 (one-way market) VIDYA behaves like a fast EMA; when CMO nears 0 it barely moves.
formula: VIDYA_t = VIDYA_{t-1} + alpha * (|CMO_t|/100) * (P_t - VIDYA_{t-1}); alpha = 2/(n+1); CMO = 100*(Su - Sd)/(Su + Sd) with Su, Sd the sums of up and down close-to-close changes over the look-back.
failure_modes: In choppy markets CMO hovers near zero and VIDYA effectively freezes, missing genuine moves; results are sensitive to the CMO look-back choice.
misconceptions: VIDYA is not the same as KAMA: KAMA adapts via an efficiency ratio (net change over path length), while VIDYA adapts via a momentum-volatility index.
example: If alpha = 0.2 and the CMO reads +60, the effective smoothing constant is 0.12; at CMO = +10 it falls to 0.02.

name: Kaufman adaptive moving average
definition: Perry Kaufman's adaptive moving average, which varies its smoothing constant with an Efficiency Ratio measuring how directional (versus noisy) recent price movement has been, hugging price in trends and going flat in chop.
intuition: An average that asks how much of the recent movement is real trend versus random wiggle, and speeds up only when the answer is mostly trend.
mechanics: ER = |Close - Close_n| / sum|Close - prior Close| over n bars (0 to 1); SC = [ER*(fast - slow) + slow]^2 with fast = 2/(2+1) and slow = 2/(30+1); KAMA_t = KAMA_{t-1} + SC*(P_t - KAMA_{t-1}). Recommended settings KAMA(10,2,30); the first value is seeded with an SMA.
failure_modes: A simple price/KAMA crossover system still whipsaws without price or time filters, and in persistently choppy markets ER stays low, leaving KAMA flat and uninformative.
misconceptions: Lengthening the ER look-back does not necessarily improve the indicator — the documented guidance is to adjust the fast (middle) parameter for smoothing, not the ER period.
example: If price rises for 10 straight bars, change equals volatility so ER = 1 and KAMA tracks a 2-period EMA; if price ends unchanged after 10 choppy bars, ER is near 0 and KAMA barely moves.

name: Zero-lag exponential moving average
definition: A lag-corrected EMA (John Ehlers and Ric Way, 'Zero Lag (Well, Almost)', TASC 2010): an EMA applied to de-lagged data — price plus the difference between the current price and the price (n-1)/2 bars ago — compensating for the EMA's inherent lag.
intuition: Pre-correct the data for the lag you know the EMA will add, so the smoothed output lands close to the current price.
mechanics: Form the adjusted series Z_t = P_t + (P_t - P_{t-lag}) with lag = floor((n-1)/2), then take a standard n-period EMA of Z. The construction is related to Mulloy's DEMA/TEMA lag-cancellation idea.
formula: lag = floor((n-1)/2); Z_t = P_t + (P_t - P_{t-lag}); ZLEMA_t = EMA_n(Z)_t with k = 2/(n+1).
failure_modes: The de-lagging term amplifies noise and overshoots on sharp reversals; in sideways markets it whipsaws more than a plain EMA.
misconceptions: Zero lag is aspirational: the correction removes the systematic EMA lag in smooth trends but cannot anticipate turning points, where lag remains.
example: For n = 10, lag = 4; if P_t = 105 and P_{t-4} = 100, the EMA is applied to 110 instead of 105, pulling the average up toward the trending price.

name: Double exponential moving average
definition: Patrick Mulloy's Double Exponential Moving Average (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, January 1994): a composite of a single and a double EMA that subtracts the extra lag of the double-smoothed series from the single-smoothed one to track price more closely.
intuition: Measure how much double-smoothing lags single-smoothing, and add that gap back to the fast EMA as a correction.
mechanics: EMA1 = EMA(price), EMA2 = EMA(EMA1); DEMA = 2*EMA1 - EMA2. The double-smoothed EMA2 serves only as a lag-correction term, not as the output. Default 20 periods; signals via price/line crosses or fast/slow DEMA crossovers, which occur earlier than equivalent EMA crossovers.
formula: DEMA = 2*EMA_n(P) - EMA_n(EMA_n(P)).
failure_modes: Greater responsiveness means more noise and more false signals in choppy markets; long-term investors may be better served by a traditional, smoother average.
misconceptions: DEMA is not simply the EMA of an EMA — that double-smoothed series alone would lag more, not less; the output is 2*EMA1 - EMA2.
example: If EMA1 = 50 and EMA2 = 48, DEMA = 2*50 - 48 = 52, pulling the average above EMA1 toward current price.

name: Triple exponential moving average
definition: Patrick Mulloy's Triple Exponential Moving Average, which extends DEMA with a third smoothing layer, combining single, double, and triple EMAs to remove even more lag for short-term trading.
intuition: DEMA with one more correction term — closer still to price, noisier still.
mechanics: TEMA = 3*EMA1 - 3*EMA2 + EMA3, where EMA2 = EMA(EMA1) and EMA3 = EMA(EMA2). Used via price crosses or fast/slow TEMA crossovers, which fire earlier than equivalent DEMA or EMA crosses; default 20 periods.
formula: TEMA = 3*EMA_n(P) - 3*EMA_n(EMA_n(P)) + EMA_n(EMA_n(EMA_n(P))).
failure_modes: Minimal lag means minimal noise filtering — it whipsaws the most of the EMA family in sideways markets, and some lag is actually useful for longer-term analysis.
misconceptions: Faster is not universally better: TEMA's responsiveness amplifies noise, so it is not a straight upgrade over EMA or DEMA. Also, TEMA is not TRIX — TRIX is the 1-period rate of change of a triple EMA.

name: Moving average crossover
definition: A signal framework in which a shorter-period moving average crossing a longer-period one (or price crossing a moving average) is read as a shift in trend direction; John Murphy calls the two-average version the double crossover method. It is an analytical convention, not a proven predictive law.
intuition: When the fast average overtakes the slow one, recent prices have moved enough to bend the trend measure — a simple, mechanical trend-change rule.
mechanics: Bullish signal: the short MA crosses above the long MA; bearish: short crosses below. Common pairs are 5/35 (short-term) and 50/200 (long-term); a triple-crossover variant uses three averages. MACD(12,26,1) quantifies EMA crossovers as the fast-minus-slow difference.
failure_modes: Both averages lag, so signals are late by construction and whipsaw repeatedly in trendless markets; the documented Home Depot example shows three whipsaws before one successful 20%+ signal.
misconceptions: A crossover describes what has already happened; it does not predict continuation. Unfiltered crossover systems are unreliable — price or time filters are typically needed.
example: A 10-day EMA crossing above a 50-day EMA is a bullish crossover; with MACD(10,50,1), the MACD line crossing zero marks the same event.

name: Golden cross
definition: A bullish moving-average crossover — classically the 50-day SMA crossing above the 200-day SMA — interpreted by technicians as confirmation of a long-term uptrend. It is a widely watched analytical convention, not a proven predictive law.
intuition: The market's medium-term average climbing above its long-term average suggests that upward momentum has been sustained long enough to matter.
mechanics: Identified on daily charts when the shorter (typically 50-day) moving average crosses up through the longer (typically 200-day) one; because both averages lag, the cross usually prints well after the actual low.
failure_modes: Late by construction and whipsaw-prone in range-bound markets; by the time a golden cross prints, much of the advance has often already occurred.
misconceptions: It is not a guaranteed buy signal or a law of markets — it records that an advance has been large and persistent; any forward-looking edge is an empirical question, not a property of the construction.
example: MACD(50,200,1) turning positive marks the same 50/200 EMA golden cross in oscillator form.

name: Death cross
definition: A bearish moving-average crossover — classically the 50-day SMA crossing below the 200-day SMA — read as confirmation of a long-term downtrend; the mirror image of the golden cross and equally a convention rather than a proven law.
intuition: The medium-term average sinking below the long-term average suggests the decline has been deep and persistent enough to bend long-term trend measures.
mechanics: The shorter (typically 50-day) moving average crosses down through the longer (typically 200-day) one; like the golden cross, it lags and typically prints well after the actual top.
failure_modes: Late and whipsaw-prone in sideways markets; many historical death crosses have occurred near market lows rather than before extended declines.
misconceptions: A death cross does not forecast a crash — it records that a decline has already been large enough to pull the 50-day average below the 200-day.
example: MACD(50,200,1) turning negative marks the same 50/200 EMA death cross in oscillator form.

name: Moving average convergence divergence
definition: Gerald Appel's Moving Average Convergence/Divergence oscillator (late 1970s): a momentum indicator built from the difference between a fast and a slow EMA (default 12 and 26) with a 9-period EMA signal line, combining trend-following and momentum information in one unbounded oscillator.
intuition: When the fast average pulls away from the slow one, momentum is accelerating; when they converge, the move is running out of steam.
mechanics: MACD line = EMA(12) - EMA(26) of closes; signal line = 9-period EMA of the MACD line; histogram = line minus signal. Signals include signal-line crossovers, zero-line (centerline) crossovers — equivalent to the underlying EMA crossover — and divergences with price.
formula: MACD = EMA_12(Close) - EMA_26(Close); Signal = EMA_9(MACD); Histogram = MACD - Signal.
failure_modes: Signal-line crossovers whipsaw in flat or volatile markets, and crossovers at extremes often mark momentum exhaustion rather than reversal; being unbounded, MACD cannot flag overbought or oversold conditions.
misconceptions: MACD is not a bounded oscillator, so high readings are not inherently overbought; nor does a signal-line cross guarantee a trend change.
example: If the 12-day EMA is 102 and the 26-day EMA is 100, MACD = +2; with a 9-day signal line at 1.5, the histogram reads +0.5.

name: MACD line
definition: The core series of the MACD: the fast (default 12-period) EMA minus the slow (default 26-period) EMA of closing prices, oscillating around zero as the two averages converge and diverge.
intuition: The spread between a fast and a slow average: positive and widening means upside momentum is building.
mechanics: Computed each bar as EMA_12(C) - EMA_26(C); it crosses zero exactly when the two EMAs cross, and its distance from zero measures how far the averages have diverged.
formula: MACD line = EMA_12(Close) - EMA_26(Close).
failure_modes: As an EMA spread it lags and whipsaws in trendless markets; absolute values are price-scale dependent and not comparable across securities (use the PPO for that).
misconceptions: A falling MACD line is not the same as falling prices — the EMA spread can shrink while prices are still rising, reflecting decelerating momentum only.
example: A 12-day EMA of 50 and a 26-day EMA of 48 give a MACD line of +2: the fast average sits 2 points above the slow one.

name: MACD signal line
definition: A 9-period EMA of the MACD line, plotted alongside it; crossovers of the MACD line through this signal line are the most common MACD trading signal.
intuition: A moving average of the MACD itself, smoothing its turns so crossovers are easier to read.
mechanics: Signal_t = EMA_9(MACD line). A bullish crossover occurs when the MACD line rises above the signal line, bearish when it falls below; because it trails the MACD line, it adds a further layer of lag.
formula: Signal = EMA_9(MACD), where MACD = EMA_12(Close) - EMA_26(Close).
failure_modes: Adds lag to an already lagging construction, and crossovers occurring at positive or negative extremes often mark exhaustion and reverse quickly.
misconceptions: The 9-period setting is a convention, not an optimum, and the signal line has no meaning independently of the MACD line it smooths.
example: If the MACD line is 2.0 and its 9-period EMA is 1.5, the MACD sits above its signal line — a post-crossover bullish state.

name: MACD histogram
definition: The bar plot of the MACD line minus its signal line, visualizing the distance between them; it expands and contracts ahead of crossovers and is used to spot momentum shifts early.
intuition: Instead of waiting for the two MACD lines to cross, watch the gap between them shrink or grow.
mechanics: Histogram = MACD - Signal; positive when MACD is above its signal line, negative below. It crosses zero exactly at a signal-line crossover, and its peaks and troughs precede the crossovers themselves.
formula: Histogram = MACD line - Signal line = (EMA_12(C) - EMA_26(C)) - EMA_9(MACD).
failure_modes: More sensitive than the lines themselves, so it flips sign more often in choppy markets; a shrinking histogram warns of a crossover but says nothing about whether that crossover will matter.
misconceptions: A declining histogram does not mean prices are falling — only that the MACD's lead over its signal line is narrowing.
example: MACD = 2.0 with signal = 1.5 gives a histogram of +0.5; if the next bar's MACD is 1.8 and signal 1.6, the histogram shrinks to +0.2, warning that upside momentum is fading.

name: Relative strength index
definition: J. Welles Wilder's momentum oscillator (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978) comparing smoothed average gains to smoothed average losses over a look-back period (default 14), bounded between 0 and 100.
intuition: A speedometer for price: it shows how persistently and strongly the market has been closing up versus down.
mechanics: RS = Average Gain / Average Loss, with first values simple 14-period means and subsequent values Wilder-smoothed ((prior*13 + current)/14); RSI = 100 - 100/(1+RS). Wilder treated readings above 70 as overbought and below 30 as oversold; also used for divergences, failure swings, and centerline analysis.
formula: RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS); RS = AvgGain / AvgLoss; AvgGain_t = (AvgGain_{t-1}*13 + Gain_t)/14 (likewise losses, expressed as positive values).
failure_modes: In strong trends RSI can stay above 70 or below 30 for extended periods, so fading overbought/oversold readings fails; bearish divergences can recur for months before any reversal.
misconceptions: Overbought does not mean the price must fall — it can signal strength. RSI is also not a comparison between two securities; that is relative strength (price relative).
example: If the 14-day average gain is 1.0 and the average loss is 0.5, RS = 2 and RSI = 100 - 100/3 = 66.7.

name: Stochastic oscillator
definition: George Lane's momentum indicator (late 1950s) measuring where the close sits within the high-low range of the look-back period, bounded 0-100 and published in Fast, Slow, and Full versions. Lane's premise: momentum changes direction before price.
intuition: In an uptrend prices tend to close near the top of their recent range; the stochastic quantifies that tendency.
mechanics: %K = (C - LL)/(HH - LL)*100 over (default) 14 periods; %D = 3-period SMA of %K acts as the signal line; the Slow version smooths %K once more. Readings above 80 are overbought, below 20 oversold; signals come from %K/%D crosses, divergences, and Lane's bull/bear set-ups.
formula: %K = 100 * (C - LL_n)/(HH_n - LL_n); %D = SMA_3(%K); HH_n and LL_n are the highest high and lowest low over n periods.
failure_modes: Can remain overbought or oversold through an entire strong trend, so counter-trend signals fail repeatedly; fast versions whipsaw, and signals work best in trading ranges or zigzag trends.
misconceptions: The stochastic does not follow price or volume — per Lane it follows the speed (momentum) of price; and an overbought reading alone is not a sell signal.
example: With a 14-day high of 110, low of 100, and close of 108, %K = (108-100)/(110-100)*100 = 80.

name: Stochastic RSI
definition: Chande and Kroll's oscillator (The New Technical Trader, 1994) that applies the stochastic formula to RSI values instead of price, measuring where the current RSI sits within its own high-low range over the look-back period; an indicator of an indicator, bounded between 0 and 1.
intuition: RSI can drift between 80 and 20 for weeks without reaching its classic extremes; StochRSI restores sensitivity by tracking RSI's position within its recent range rather than its absolute level.
mechanics: Compute n-period RSI, then take (RSI - lowest RSI over n) / (highest RSI over n - lowest RSI over n), with n typically 14. A value of 1 means RSI is at its n-period high, 0 at its low; some platforms scale it to 0-100 and smooth it with short moving averages.
formula: StochRSI = (RSI - min(RSI, n)) / (max(RSI, n) - min(RSI, n)), with RSI and the range window typically both 14 periods.
failure_modes: Two transformations removed from price, it is very jumpy and whipsaws frequently; in strong trends it pins at 0 or 1 for long stretches, issuing repeated false reversal alerts.
misconceptions: An overbought StochRSI reading is not a sell signal by itself - Chande and Kroll used 0.80/0.20 extremes within a trend context, and readings can stay extreme while the trend continues.
example: If 14-day RSI has ranged from 30 to 70 over the last 14 days and current RSI is 50, StochRSI = (50-30)/(70-30) = 0.5.

name: Williams percent R
definition: Larry Williams' momentum oscillator showing where the close sits relative to the highest high of the look-back period, plotted on an inverted 0 to -100 scale; mathematically the inverse of the fast stochastic %K line.
intuition: It answers 'how close is the latest close to the top of the recent range?': readings near 0 mean closes at the range top, readings near -100 mean closes at the bottom.
mechanics: Subtract the close from the highest high of the last n periods (default 14), divide by the high-low range, and multiply by -100. Readings from 0 to -20 are conventionally overbought, -80 to -100 oversold; the -50 centerline and momentum failures (failed retests of -20) give additional signals.
formula: %R = ((HighestHigh(n) - Close) / (HighestHigh(n) - LowestLow(n))) x -100, default n = 14.
failure_modes: Like all range-position oscillators it sticks at extremes during strong trends and whipsaws across the -50 centerline in choppy markets.
misconceptions: Overbought (above -20) does not mean sell: sustained closes near the top of the range signal persistent buying pressure, and %R can stay overbought through an entire uptrend.
example: Highest high 110, lowest low 100, close 103: %R = ((110-103)/10) x -100 = -70; a close at 108 gives -20.

name: Rate of change
definition: A pure momentum oscillator measuring the percentage change between the current close and the close n periods ago, plotted as an unbounded line around zero; the StockCharts ROC page notes the indicator is also referred to simply as Momentum.
intuition: It is rise over run for prices: positive while the price is higher than n periods ago, negative while lower, with distance from zero showing how fast the move is.
mechanics: Compute (Close - Close n periods ago) / (Close n periods ago) x 100, default n = 12. Used for zero-line trend bias, security-specific overbought/oversold extremes (often +/-10%), and divergences.
formula: ROC(n) = ((C_t - C_{t-n}) / C_{t-n}) x 100, where C_t is the current close.
failure_modes: Zero-line crosses whipsaw in ranges, and divergences fail often because strong trends frequently start with the sharpest ROC spike, printing a bearish divergence mid-advance.
misconceptions: A falling ROC is not a falling price - price still rises as long as ROC is positive; it only means the advance is decelerating.
example: Close today 55, close 12 days ago 50: ROC = (55-50)/50 x 100 = +10%.

name: Momentum indicator
definition: The simplest momentum measure: the absolute point difference between the current close and the close n periods ago, plotted as an unbounded oscillator around zero; the unscaled sibling of the rate-of-change, which expresses the same comparison as a percentage.
intuition: It tracks how many points price gained or lost over the window, ignoring the price level, so its slope shows acceleration or deceleration of the move.
mechanics: Compute Close - Close(n periods ago), conventionally with n around 10-14. Positive values show net gains over the window, negative values net losses; zero-line crosses define the momentum bias.
formula: Momentum(n) = C_t - C_{t-n}; the percentage variant is ROC(n) = ((C_t - C_{t-n}) / C_{t-n}) x 100.
failure_modes: Being unscaled in points, readings are not comparable across securities or across large price changes in one security; like ROC it whipsaws around zero in sideways markets.
misconceptions: Momentum indicators describe past speed; a high positive reading can persist or reverse without warning and is not a prediction of continued gains.
example: Close today 55, close 12 days ago 50: momentum = +5 points, whereas the rate of change is +10%.

name: Commodity channel index
definition: Donald Lambert's oscillator (Commodities magazine, 1980) measuring how far the typical price has deviated from its moving average, expressed in units of mean absolute deviation scaled by 0.015 so that roughly 70-80% of readings fall between -100 and +100.
intuition: CCI normalizes 'how stretched is price from its own average?' - excursions beyond +/-100 mark statistically unusual strength or weakness that can flag a new trend or an extreme.
mechanics: Compute the typical price TP = (H+L+C)/3, subtract its n-period SMA (default 20), and divide by 0.015 times the mean absolute deviation of TP from that SMA. Used for +/-100 trend-emergence signals, +/-200 extremes, and confirmed divergences.
formula: CCI = (TP - SMA(TP, n)) / (0.015 x MeanDev), TP = (High + Low + Close)/3, MeanDev = (1/n) x sum of |TP_i - SMA(TP, n)| over the last n periods.
failure_modes: CCI is unbounded, so overbought/oversold levels are arbitrary and must be calibrated per security; zero-line crosses whipsaw, and in strong trends CCI stays beyond +/-100 while price keeps running.
misconceptions: Despite the name it is not commodity-specific, and +/-100 is a statistical convention, not a hard ceiling - the oscillator routinely exceeds it.
example: TP = 24, 20-period SMA of TP = 22, mean deviation 1.33: CCI = (24-22)/(0.015 x 1.33) ~ +100.

name: Average directional index
definition: Welles Wilder's trend-strength gauge (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): the Wilder-smoothed average of the Directional Movement Index (DX), which measures the spread between +DI and -DI relative to their sum; ADX quantifies trend strength on a 0-100 scale regardless of direction.
intuition: ADX answers 'is the market trending at all?', not which way - Wilder suggested readings above 25 indicate a strong trend and below 20 the absence of one.
mechanics: Compute +DM, -DM and True Range, smooth each with Wilder's technique over 14 periods, derive +DI and -DI, then DX = 100 x |+DI - -DI| / (+DI + -DI); ADX is the 14-period Wilder-smoothed average of DX. Roughly 150 periods of data are needed for stable values.
formula: DX = 100 x |+DI14 - -DI14| / (+DI14 + -DI14); first ADX = 14-period average of DX, then ADX_t = ((ADX_{t-1} x 13) + DX_t) / 14.
failure_modes: Heavy double smoothing makes ADX very laggy - it often confirms a trend only near its end; it cannot distinguish up from down, and in flat markets it offers no usable signal.
misconceptions: A rising ADX does not mean prices are rising - ADX also rises in strong downtrends; and a falling ADX means the trend is weakening, not that it has reversed.
example: If +DI = 32 and -DI = 12, DX = 100 x 20/44 ~ 45.5; sustained DX values near this level push ADX above 25, Wilder's strong-trend threshold.

name: Positive directional indicator
definition: The positive half of Wilder's Directional Movement System: 100 times the ratio of smoothed positive directional movement (upward range expansion beyond the prior bar's high) to smoothed True Range over 14 periods, measuring the strength of upside directional movement.
intuition: +DI tracks how much of the recent true-range movement was upside expansion; when +DI is above -DI, buyers hold the directional edge.
mechanics: +DM = current high minus prior high when that exceeds the prior-low-minus-current-low move and is positive, else 0 (inside bars give 0). Smooth +DM and TR with Wilder's method; +DI = 100 x smoothed +DM / smoothed TR. Crosses of +DI above -DI are buy signals, conventionally filtered by ADX above 20-25.
formula: +DI14 = 100 x (Wilder-smoothed +DM14) / (Wilder-smoothed TR14); +DM = max(High_t - High_{t-1}, 0) if High_t - High_{t-1} > Low_{t-1} - Low_t, else 0.
failure_modes: Inside bars force +DM to zero and +DI/-DI crosses whipsaw badly in flat markets; Wilder's smoothing lag means crosses often come well after the move began.
misconceptions: +DI measures relative directional movement, not the probability of further gains; a +DI > -DI cross without trend strength (ADX) is a weak signal - StockCharts notes many such crosses invalidate.
example: Today's high 52 vs prior 50 (+2) while lows moved down only 0.5: +DM = 2; if the smoothed +DM is 20 against a smoothed TR of 100, +DI = 20.

name: Negative directional indicator
definition: The negative half of Wilder's Directional Movement System: 100 times the ratio of smoothed negative directional movement (downward range expansion beyond the prior bar's low) to smoothed True Range over 14 periods, measuring the strength of downside directional movement.

name: Average true range
definition: Welles Wilder's volatility measure (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): the Wilder-smoothed average of True Range, where True Range is the greatest of the current high-low span, |high - prior close|, and |low - prior close| - capturing gap and limit-move volatility that a plain high-low range misses.
intuition: ATR tells you how much an instrument typically moves per bar, with no directional content: it expands in violent markets and contracts in quiet ones.
mechanics: TR_t = max(High - Low, |High - Close_prev|, |Low - Close_prev|). The first 14-period ATR is the SMA of the first 14 TR values; thereafter ATR_t = (ATR_{t-1} x 13 + TR_t) / 14. Used for stop distances, position sizing, and breakout validation.
failure_modes: ATR is in absolute price units, so values are not comparable across securities or across large price changes in one security; the recursive Wilder smoothing makes early values seed-dependent and needs long histories (StockCharts calculates back 250+ periods) to stabilize.
misconceptions: ATR says nothing about direction - a falling ATR during a rally is not bearish, just quietening; and a high ATR is not by itself a top signal.
example: StockCharts' spreadsheet: the first 14-day ATR comes out at 0.56, and ATR surged as QQQ plunged with long candlesticks in May.

name: Bollinger Bands
definition: John Bollinger's volatility bands: a 20-period simple moving average flanked by upper and lower bands set k standard deviations (default 2) of price above and below it, so the envelope widens as volatility rises and contracts as it falls.
intuition: The bands define 'relatively high' and 'relatively low' statistically: price at the upper band is high relative to recent volatility, at the lower band relatively low - without implying a reversal by itself.
mechanics: Middle band = SMA(20); upper = middle + k x sigma(20), lower = middle - k x sigma(20), where sigma is the 20-period standard deviation of price (same window as the SMA). Bollinger suggests k = 2.1 for 50-period and 1.9 for 10-period settings. Used for band tags, M-top/W-bottom confirmation, and the Squeeze via BandWidth.
formula: Middle = SMA(P, 20); Upper = Middle + k x StdDev(P, 20); Lower = Middle - k x StdDev(P, 20); k = 2 by default.
failure_modes: Band touches are 'tags', not signals: in strong trends price walks the band for long stretches, and the SMA base lags; squeezes flag volatility compression but give no direction, and post-squeeze breaks can be head-fakes.
misconceptions: A tag of the upper band is not an automatic sell - 'relatively high' is not 'about to fall'; nor do the bands contain a normal distribution's 95% of prices, since returns are not normal (Bollinger cites 88-89% empirically).
example: SMA(20) = 50 with sigma = 1.5: upper band = 53, lower = 47; a close at 53.4 is above the band - a tag, not a signal.

name: Bollinger bandwidth
definition: A Bollinger-derived indicator measuring the percentage width between the upper and lower bands relative to the middle band, tracking volatility expansion and contraction on a normalized scale comparable across securities and timeframes.
intuition: It turns the visual 'pinch' of the bands into a number: falling BandWidth means volatility is drying up; the famous Squeeze is BandWidth at the low end of its own historical range.
mechanics: Compute (Upper - Lower) / Middle x 100 from the Bollinger Bands (default 20, 2). Narrowness is judged against the indicator's own 6-12 month range; the Squeeze alerts to coming volatility, and the direction comes from the subsequent band break.
formula: BandWidth = ((UpperBand - LowerBand) / MiddleBand) x 100.
failure_modes: 'Narrow' is relative to each security's own history, so thresholds do not transfer between instruments; the Squeeze is directionless and the first band break after a squeeze can fail.
misconceptions: A low BandWidth does not guarantee an imminent big move - volatility can stay compressed for months, and low-volatility securities always show lower BandWidth than volatile ones.
example: Upper 53, lower 47, middle 50: BandWidth = (53-47)/50 x 100 = 12; StockCharts' Alaska Airlines squeeze triggered below a BandWidth of 10.

name: Percent B
definition: A Bollinger-derived indicator expressing the close's position within the bands as a percentage of band width: 100 at the upper band, 0 at the lower band, 50 at the middle band, and beyond those values when price is outside the bands.
intuition: %B states exactly where price sits inside the Bollinger envelope, making band tags, divergences and pattern confirmations quantifiable and comparable across securities.
mechanics: Compute (Price - LowerBand) / (UpperBand - LowerBand) x 100 using the standard (20, 2) bands. Values above 100 mean closes above the upper band, below 0 below the lower band; used for walking-the-bands trend confirmation and W-bottom/M-top pattern work.
formula: %B = ((P - LowerBand) / (UpperBand - LowerBand)) x 100, with bands from Bollinger Bands(20, 2) by default.
failure_modes: Inherits the Bollinger SMA's lag, and readings above 100 can persist through an entire uptrend, so extremes are weak standalone timing signals.
misconceptions: %B above 100 is not an automatic overbought-sell reading - upper-band tags in uptrends indicate strength; interpretation depends on trend and pattern context.
example: Bands 47-53 with a close at 50: %B = (50-47)/(53-47) x 100 = 50; a close at 53.6 gives %B = 110.

name: Keltner Channel
definition: Volatility envelopes around an exponential moving average, with channel lines set a multiple of Average True Range above and below the EMA; the modern version popularized by Linda Raschke replaces Chester Keltner's 1960 10-day typical-price SMA plus/minus high-low range with EMA plus/minus ATR.
intuition: Like Bollinger Bands but built from ATR instead of standard deviation, Keltner Channels are smoother and more constant in width, which suits trend identification and breakout detection.
mechanics: Middle line = EMA(20); upper = EMA + m x ATR(10), lower = EMA - m x ATR(10), with m = 2 by default. A close outside the channel signals extraordinary strength or weakness; a flat channel marks a range where the lines serve as overbought/oversold references.
formula: Upper = EMA(P, 20) + 2 x ATR(10); Lower = EMA(P, 20) - 2 x ATR(10).
failure_modes: Trend-following at heart, it lags and whipsaws in flat markets; original (SMA +/- range) and modern (EMA +/- ATR) versions differ, so values are not comparable across platforms without checking the convention.
misconceptions: A close beyond the channel is not an automatic fade - it more often marks the start of a trend move than an exhaustion.
example: EMA(20) = 100 and ATR(10) = 2: upper channel = 104, lower = 96; a close at 105 is an upside channel breakout.

name: Donchian Channel
definition: Richard Donchian's price channel plotting the highest high and lowest low of the last n periods (commonly 20) as upper and lower bands, with an optional midline at their average; the basis of classic breakout systems such as the Turtle Traders' rules.
intuition: The channel shows the extremes of the recent trading range; a close outside it is by definition a new n-period high or low, which breakout traders treat as trend initiation.
mechanics: Upper = max(High, n); Lower = min(Low, n); Middle = (Upper + Lower)/2. Breakouts beyond the bands generate trend-following signals, and the channel width reads volatility; the bands also serve as trailing stop and support/resistance references.
formula: UC = max(High, N); LC = min(Low, N); Middle = (UC + LC)/2, typically N = 20.
failure_modes: False breakouts are common in sideways markets where price repeatedly pokes the bands; as a purely lagging construction it gives no warning before the breakout occurs.
misconceptions: Touching the upper band is not 'overbought' - it is a new n-period high, the exact condition trend-followers buy; the channel records extremes, it does not predict them.
example: 20-day high 105, low 95: upper band 105, lower 95, midline 100; a close at 106 is an upside breakout.

name: Standard deviation channel
definition: A channel built on a least-squares linear regression line through the last n closes, with parallel upper and lower lines plotted a set number of standard deviations (typically 2) of price away from the regression line.
intuition: The regression line is the best-fit trend through the window and the bands mark statistically typical deviation around it - about two-thirds of observations within +/-1 sigma if deviations were normal.
mechanics: Fit y = a + mx to the last n closes by least squares, compute the standard deviation of closes over the window, and plot the regression line with parallel lines offset by +/-k sigma (k = 2 default). The slope gives trend direction and the width gives volatility; it generates no signals by itself.
formula: Center: y(x) = a + mx from the least-squares fit over n bars; Upper = y + k x sigma, Lower = y - k x sigma, sigma = standard deviation of the n closes, k typically 2.
failure_modes: The channel is refit every bar, so historical channel lines repaint and backtests on drawn channels are unreliable; the symmetric deviation assumption fails in trending or fat-tailed markets.
misconceptions: Unlike Bollinger Bands the center is a regression line, not a moving average, and price does not owe a return to it - in strong trends price rides one side of the channel.
example: A 40-bar regression of closes gives y = 98 + 0.1x with sigma = 1.2; at the last bar the center is 102, the 2-sigma upper band 104.4 and the lower 99.6.

name: Moving average envelope
definition: Parallel bands set a fixed percentage above and below a simple or exponential moving average, creating a constant-width channel used for trend confirmation and, in flat markets, as overbought/oversold references.
intuition: Unlike volatility-adaptive bands, the percentage offset never changes, so a touch of the envelope always means 'price is x% stretched from its average.'
mechanics: Upper = MA x (1 + p), Lower = MA x (1 - p), e.g., a 20-day SMA with p = 2.5%. Parameters must be chosen per security volatility - indexes need narrow envelopes (2-3%), volatile stocks wide ones (5-10%).
formula: Upper = MA(n) x (1 + p); Lower = MA(n) x (1 - p); e.g., MA = SMA(20), p = 0.025.
failure_modes: The fixed width does not adapt: too narrow in volatility expansions (constant false breaks) and too wide in quiet periods (no signals at all); it also inherits the base average's lag.
misconceptions: Envelope breaks in a strong trend are signs of strength, not fade setups; overbought/oversold logic applies mainly when the trend is flat.
example: A 20-day SMA of 40 with 2.5% envelopes plots the upper band at 41.0 and the lower at 39.0.

name: Parabolic SAR
definition: Welles Wilder's stop-and-reverse system (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): a trailing stop plotted as dots below price in uptrends and above price in downtrends, accelerating toward price as the trend extends and flipping sides when price crosses it.
intuition: It behaves like a trailing stop that tightens the longer a trend runs - the acceleration factor pulls the dots toward price, forcing an exit when momentum stalls.
mechanics: SAR_{t+1} = SAR_t + AF x (EP - SAR_t) for uptrends (minus for downtrends), where EP is the trend's extreme point and AF starts at 0.02, stepping up 0.02 on each new extreme to a cap of 0.20. The SAR is clamped so it never enters the prior two bars' range; a price touch flips trend direction.
formula: Rising: SAR_{t+1} = SAR_t + AF x (EP - SAR_t); Falling: SAR_{t+1} = SAR_t - AF x (SAR_t - EP); AF: start 0.02, +0.02 per new EP, max 0.20.
failure_modes: Wilder himself estimated markets trend only about 30% of the time; in ranges SAR whipsaws constantly, and its always-in-the-market design has no neutral state.
misconceptions: SAR is a stop-and-reverse mechanism, not a prediction of reversal - a flip only says price crossed the trailing stop.
example: Prior SAR 48.28, extreme point 49.20, AF 0.14: new SAR = 48.13 + 0.14 x (49.20 - 48.13) = 48.28 (StockCharts' worked example).

name: Supertrend
definition: An ATR-based trend-following overlay (Olivier Seban, 2009) that plots a single line below price in uptrends and above it in downtrends, at a distance of multiplier x ATR from the bar midpoint, flipping sides when price closes through the line.
intuition: It is a volatility-adjusted trailing stop: wider when the market is volatile, tighter when calm, so ordinary noise does not stop you out but a genuine reversal does.
mechanics: Basic upper band = (H+L)/2 + m x ATR(n), basic lower = (H+L)/2 - m x ATR(n), with common defaults n = 10, m = 3. Final bands are ratcheted - the upper band can only fall and the lower only rise - until a close crosses the active band, which flips the trend state.
formula: Upper = (High + Low)/2 + Multiplier x ATR(n); Lower = (High + Low)/2 - Multiplier x ATR(n); ATR(n) = (ATR_prev x (n-1) + TR)/n (Wilder smoothing).
failure_modes: Lagging by construction and whipsaw-prone in sideways markets; it signals direction only - not trend strength - and results are sensitive to the (period, multiplier) choice.
misconceptions: A green (uptrend) line is not a standalone buy recommendation, and the plotted line is a stop level, not a price target.
example: High 20.23, low 19.04, ATR 1.15, multiplier 1: upper band = 19.635 + 1.15 = 20.79, lower = 18.48 (Investopedia's worked example).

name: Ichimoku Kinko Hyo
definition: Goichi Hosoda's 'one-look equilibrium chart' (published 1969): a five-line system of high-low midpoint averages - Conversion Line, Base Line, two Leading Spans forming the cloud (Kumo), and a Lagging Span - designed to show trend, momentum, and support/resistance at a glance.
intuition: Price above the cloud means uptrend, below means downtrend, inside means no trend; the cloud projected ahead sketches where support or resistance is expected to lie.
mechanics: Tenkan-sen = midpoint of the 9-period high-low; Kijun-sen = 26-period midpoint; Senkou A = average of the two, plotted 26 bars ahead; Senkou B = 52-period midpoint, also 26 ahead; Chikou = close plotted 26 back. Signals combine price/cloud position, cloud color (A vs B), Tenkan-Kijun crosses, and price-Kijun crosses.
formula: Tenkan = (max(H,9)+min(L,9))/2; Kijun = (max(H,26)+min(L,26))/2; Senkou A = (Tenkan+Kijun)/2 shifted +26; Senkou B = (max(H,52)+min(L,52))/2 shifted +26; Chikou = Close shifted -26.
failure_modes: Midpoint averages lag like all trend tools and whipsaw in ranges; the cloud shifted 'into the future' is computed entirely from past data and is not a forecast.
misconceptions: Ichimoku is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive system - and the 9/26/52 defaults reflect the 1960s Japanese six-day trading week, not universal constants.
example: 9-day high 55, low 51: Tenkan-sen = 53; with a 26-day midpoint of 50, Senkou A plotted 26 days ahead = 51.5.

name: Tenkan-sen
definition: The fastest Ichimoku line: the midpoint of the 9-period high-low range, (9-period high + 9-period low)/2, used as the short-term equilibrium level and the faster line in Ichimoku crossover signals.
intuition: Rather than averaging closes, it averages the range extremes, so it sits at the center of recent price action and flattens immediately when the market goes quiet.
mechanics: Compute (max(High,9) + min(Low,9))/2 each bar. A Tenkan cross above Kijun-sen is the classic bullish momentum signal (and below, bearish), conventionally filtered by price position relative to the cloud.
formula: Tenkan-sen = (max(High, 9) + min(Low, 9)) / 2.
failure_modes: As a 9-period range midpoint it moves in steps whenever the extreme bar rolls out of the window, and it whipsaws around Kijun-sen in flat markets.
misconceptions: It is not a 9-period moving average of closes - it tracks the range midpoint, so it behaves differently (steppy, bounded by extremes) from an SMA or EMA.
example: If the last 9 bars posted a highest high of 108 and a lowest low of 100, Tenkan-sen = 104.

name: Kijun-sen
definition: The slower Ichimoku line: the midpoint of the 26-period high-low range, serving as the medium-term equilibrium level, signal-confirmation line, and a common trailing reference.
intuition: It marks the recent balance point of the market; price far above it is extended, and pullbacks to a flat Kijun are watched as equilibrium tests.
mechanics: Compute (max(High,26) + min(Low,26))/2 each bar. Price-Kijun crosses and Tenkan-Kijun crosses generate Ichimoku momentum signals, while the Kijun's slope and flatness gauge the medium-term trend.
formula: Kijun-sen = (max(High, 26) + min(Low, 26)) / 2.
failure_modes: Stepwise movement and lag; in ranges price crosses it repeatedly with no follow-through.
misconceptions: A touch of the Kijun is not automatically support - it is only the midpoint of the last 26 bars' range.

name: Senkou Span A
definition: The faster cloud boundary: the average of Tenkan-sen and Kijun-sen, plotted 26 periods ahead of the current bar, forming the top of the Kumo (cloud) when above Senkou Span B and the bottom when below it.
intuition: It averages the short and medium equilibria and projects them forward, marking the near edge of expected future support or resistance.

name: Senkou Span B
definition: The slower cloud boundary: the midpoint of the 52-period high-low range, plotted 26 periods ahead, forming the long-term equilibrium edge of the Kumo.
intuition: The slowest Ichimoku line, it moves rarely and marks durable long-term balance; flat, thick sections of cloud built on Span B are watched as major support or resistance.
mechanics: Senkou Span B = (max(High,52) + min(Low,52))/2, shifted 26 bars forward. Its relation to Senkou Span A sets the cloud color, and a price break through a Span-B-defined cloud edge signals a trend change.
formula: Senkou Span B = (max(High, 52) + min(Low, 52)) / 2, plotted 26 periods into the future.
failure_modes: Extreme inertia: it can sit far from price for months, making cloud-break signals late; like all Ichimoku lines it is descriptive, not predictive.
misconceptions: A thick cloud is often called 'strong support/resistance', but that is a practitioner heuristic, not a tested law.
example: With a 52-bar high of 112 and low of 90, Senkou Span B = 101, plotted 26 bars ahead.

name: Chikou Span
definition: The Ichimoku confirmation line: today's close plotted 26 periods back on the chart, so it can be compared directly with where price and the cloud stood 26 bars ago.
intuition: By shifting the close into the past, you see at a glance whether the current price is above or below the price and cloud of 26 periods ago - a built-in momentum comparison.
mechanics: Plot Close_t at chart position t-26. Standard confirmation rules: bullish when the Chikou is above the price of 26 bars ago (and ideally above the past cloud), bearish when below.
formula: Chikou Span_t = Close_t, displayed at bar t - 26 (default displacement 26).
failure_modes: It is purely a displaced close and adds no information beyond a 26-period momentum comparison; the rightmost 26 bars of any chart show no Chikou at all.
misconceptions: Despite being drawn through past prices it is not a forecast line - it simply re-displays the close offset backward.
example: If today's close is 105 and the close 26 bars ago was 98, the Chikou point sits above that past price - a bullish confirmation.

name: On-balance volume
definition: Joe Granville's cumulative volume indicator (Granville's New Key to Stock Market Profits, 1963): a running total that adds the period's volume when the close rises and subtracts it when the close falls, tracking cumulative buying versus selling pressure.
intuition: Granville's thesis is that volume precedes price - if volume consistently flows in on up days, the OBV line rises even before price breaks out.
mechanics: OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} + volume when close_t > close_{t-1}, minus volume when lower, unchanged when equal. The absolute level is meaningless; the line's trend, divergences from price, and support/resistance breaks are the signals.
formula: OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} + sign(C_t - C_{t-1}) x V_t (no change when closes are equal).
failure_modes: A single huge-volume day permanently shifts the line, distorting later readings; it ignores intraday position, so a gap-down day closing near its high still counts as all-negative volume.
misconceptions: OBV's absolute value is not meaningful - only its direction and pattern matter; and a rising OBV does not guarantee price will follow.
example: From OBV 100,000: an up close on 8,200 shares takes it to 108,200, and a subsequent down day on 6,000 shares brings it to 102,200.

name: Accumulation distribution line
definition: Marc Chaikin's cumulative money-flow line: each period's volume is weighted by where the close falls within the high-low range (the Money Flow Multiplier) and added to a running total, measuring cumulative buying and selling pressure.
intuition: Closing near the high on big volume means buyers dominated the session; the A/D line accumulates that evidence and often diverges from price before reversals.
mechanics: Money Flow Multiplier = ((C - L) - (H - C)) / (H - L), ranging from +1 (close on the high) to -1 (close on the low); Money Flow Volume = multiplier x volume; ADL is the running sum of Money Flow Volume. Used for trend confirmation and divergences.
formula: MFM = ((C - L) - (H - C)) / (H - L); MFV = MFM x V; ADL_t = ADL_{t-1} + MFV_t.
failure_modes: It ignores close-to-close gaps: a stock that gaps down 5% but closes near the day's high still registers accumulation, so the line can disconnect from price reality.
misconceptions: Unlike OBV it does not score a day all-or-nothing; and a rising A/D line is evidence of accumulation, not a promise of higher prices.
example: H 50, L 48, C 49.5: multiplier = ((49.5-48) - (50-49.5))/2 = 0.5; on 10,000 shares the Money Flow Volume is +5,000.

name: Chaikin money flow
definition: Marc Chaikin's oscillator version of the Accumulation/Distribution concept: the sum of Money Flow Volume over n periods (typically 20 or 21) divided by the sum of volume, oscillating between +1 and -1 around a zero line.
intuition: It compresses the A/D logic into a fixed window: positive CMF means closes have clustered in the upper half of their ranges, volume-weighted, over the look-back.
mechanics: Compute the Money Flow Multiplier and Money Flow Volume exactly as for the A/D line; CMF(n) = sum of MFV over n periods / sum of volume over n periods. Zero-line crosses (often buffered at +/-0.05) and divergences are the standard signals.
formula: CMF(n) = sum(MFM_i x V_i, n) / sum(V_i, n), where MFM = ((C - L) - (H - C)) / (H - L).
failure_modes: Whipsaws around the zero line in choppy markets and inherits the A/D gap blind spot - a down-gap that closes near the high reads as positive money flow.
misconceptions: Readings near +1 or -1 are essentially impossible (they would need 20 straight closes on the high or low); typical range is about +/-0.5, so small values are noise, not signal.
example: Over 20 days, if Money Flow Volume sums to 2,000,000 on total volume of 10,000,000, CMF = +0.20, indicating net buying pressure.

name: Money flow index
definition: Gene Quong and Avrum Soudack's volume-weighted momentum oscillator: an RSI-style 0-100 calculation applied to typical-price money flows, so both the direction and the volume of each bar feed the reading.
intuition: It is RSI with volume mixed in - an overbought reading requires not just rising prices but rising prices backed by rising dollar volume.
mechanics: Typical price = (H+L+C)/3; raw money flow = typical price x volume, classified positive or negative by the change in typical price; MFI = 100 - 100/(1 + positive sum / negative sum) over 14 periods. Conventional overbought above 80 (truly extreme above 90), oversold below 20 (below 10).
formula: MFI = 100 - 100/(1 + MoneyRatio); MoneyRatio = sum(PositiveMF, 14) / sum(NegativeMF, 14); RawMF = TypicalPrice x Volume; TP = (H+L+C)/3.
failure_modes: In strong trends it pins above 80 or below 20 while price continues; volume spikes (expiry days, index rebalancing) distort it without any change in sentiment.
misconceptions: MFI overbought is not a sell signal - the creators recommended the stricter 90/10 levels precisely because 80/20 fires too often in trends; and MFI is not interchangeable with RSI, since volume can make them diverge.
example: If 14-day positive money flow is 120M and negative is 60M, the ratio is 2 and MFI = 100 - 100/3 ~ 66.7.

name: Ease of movement
definition: Richard Arms' oscillator relating midpoint change to volume and range: it measures how much price moved per unit of volume, rising when prices advance with ease (large range, light volume) and falling when they decline with ease.
intuition: If a big price move needs little volume, movement is 'easy'; if heavy volume produces a tiny range, movement is labored - EMV quantifies the effort-versus-result idea behind Arms' Equivolume charts.
mechanics: Distance moved = midpoint_t - midpoint_{t-1} with midpoint = (H+L)/2; Box ratio = (V / 100,000,000) / (H - L); 1-period EMV = distance / box ratio; the traded indicator is a 14-period SMA of 1-period EMV. Positive readings mean rising with ease, negative falling with ease.
formula: EMV = ((H+L)/2 - (H_prev+L_prev)/2) / ((V/100,000,000)/(H-L)); EMV(14) = SMA(1-period EMV, 14); the volume scale divisor is platform-dependent.
failure_modes: The volume scale divisor is arbitrary and platform-dependent, so absolute values are not comparable across platforms; tiny-range or low-volume bars make the ratio explode into spikes.
misconceptions: A high positive EMV is not automatically bullish strength - it can simply mean price drifted up on falling volume, which many traders read as weakness.
example: If the midpoint rises 1.00 on volume of 20M and a range of 2.00, the box ratio is 0.2/2 = 0.1 and 1-period EMV = 10.0 - an 'easy' advance.

name: Force index
definition: Alexander Elder's oscillator (Trading for a Living) multiplying the close-to-close price change by volume, combining direction, extent, and participation into one measure of the force behind a move; the smoothed 13-period EMA form is the standard version.
intuition: A one-point gain on huge volume shows more conviction than the same gain on a trickle - Force Index scores moves by both size and participation.
mechanics: Force(1) = (Close_t - Close_{t-1}) x Volume_t; Force(13) = 13-period EMA of Force(1). Used for trend confirmation at the zero line, divergences, and - in Elder's pullback system - a 2-period Force Index against a 22-day EMA trend filter.
formula: FI(1) = (Close_t - Close_{t-1}) x Volume_t; FI(13) = EMA(FI(1), 13).
failure_modes: The raw 1-period version is extremely jagged and the smoothed version lags; because it is price change times volume in absolute terms, values are not comparable across securities.
misconceptions: A positive Force Index does not mean buyers are 'in control' going forward - it records that the last bars rose on volume, which can reverse immediately.
example: A close rising from 50.00 to 50.84 on 162,619 shares gives Force(1) = 0.84 x 162,619 ~ +136,600, the largest reading in StockCharts' Pfizer example.

name: Negative volume index
definition: Paul Dysart's cumulative index (1930s; popularized by Norman Fosback in Stock Market Logic) that accumulates percentage price changes only on periods when volume declines, on the theory that informed 'smart money' acts on quiet days while the crowd trades on high-volume days.
intuition: Strip out the noisy high-volume days and watch what remains: if price grinds higher on falling-volume days, quiet accumulation is presumed.
mechanics: Fosback's version (used by StockCharts): start the index at 1000; when volume falls versus the prior period, apply the period's percentage price change to the index; when volume rises, leave it unchanged. Signals come from NVI relative to its 255-day EMA - above it favors a bull market, below it a bear market.
formula: If V_t < V_{t-1}: NVI_t = NVI_{t-1} x (1 + (C_t - C_{t-1})/C_{t-1}); else NVI_t = NVI_{t-1}. Dysart's original accumulated net market advances instead of percentage price change.
failure_modes: Designed for broad market indexes with exchange volume, it behaves erratically on individual stocks; the 255-day EMA signal lags heavily and whipsaws in volatile stretches.
misconceptions: Fosback's 96%/53% bull/bear odds were results from a 1941-1975 study, not stable laws; and falling volume is not inherently bullish in every market regime.
example: From NVI 1000: volume falls and price rises 0.8%, so NVI = 1008; next day volume rises and price rises 1%, and NVI stays 1008.

name: Positive volume index
definition: The complement of the Negative Volume Index: Dysart's cumulative index (in Fosback's formulation) that accumulates percentage price changes only on periods when volume increases, tracking what the volume-driven 'crowd' is doing.
intuition: High-volume days are when the crowd trades; PVI isolates those days to show the crowd's cumulative net effect on price.
mechanics: When today's volume exceeds yesterday's, add the percentage price change (scaled by the index) to the running PVI from a base of 1000; otherwise the index is unchanged. Watched against its 255-period (one-year) moving average: above it confirms rising prices, below it confirms declines.
formula: If V_t > V_{t-1}: PVI_t = PVI_{t-1} + ((C_t - C_{t-1})/C_{t-1}) x PVI_{t-1}; else PVI_t = PVI_{t-1}.
failure_modes: Prone to whipsaw crossovers of its moving average, and it can fall while price rises strongly if the biggest-volume days are down days; the crowd-is-wrong premise is a heuristic, not an established fact.
misconceptions: Fosback's 67%/21% bear-market odds are period-specific historical results, and PVI above its one-year average 'confirms' rather than predicts a price rise.
example: From PVI 1000: volume jumps and price rises 1.2%, so PVI = 1012; next day volume falls and price drops 0.5%, and PVI stays 1012.

name: Volume-weighted average price
definition: The average price of a security weighted by volume, computed intraday as cumulative (typical price x volume) divided by cumulative volume from the session open; the benchmark institutions use to judge execution quality and intraday fair value.
intuition: It is the day's center of gravity of trading: above VWAP the average buyer is in profit, below it the average seller is.
mechanics: For each intraday bar compute the typical price (H+L+C)/3, multiply by volume, and keep running totals of price-volume and volume; VWAP = cumulative TPV / cumulative volume, resetting each session. Price above VWAP reads as intraday strength; the line serves as a trend and mean-reversion reference.
formula: VWAP = sum(TypicalPrice_i x Volume_i) / sum(Volume_i), TypicalPrice = (High + Low + Close)/3, accumulated from the day's open.
failure_modes: Being cumulative, its lag grows through the day and early values are erratic on few bars; in its classic single-session form it is undefined for multi-day analysis.
misconceptions: VWAP is not a moving average and is not defined for daily or weekly charts; and trading 'back to VWAP' is a heuristic, not a law of price behavior.
example: StockCharts' IBM example: over the first 30 one-minute bars prices ranged 126.67-127.36 while VWAP ran 127.09-127.21 through the middle.

name: Anchored VWAP
definition: Volume-weighted average price computed from a user-chosen anchor bar - a significant high or low, earnings release, gap, or other event - rather than the session open, extending the VWAP logic across days and timeframes.
intuition: Markets reprice after events; anchoring VWAP to the event measures whether buyers or sellers have won all the volume traded since that moment.
mechanics: Same formula as VWAP - sum(TP x V) / sum(V) - but accumulation starts at the chosen anchor bar and runs to the latest bar, on any timeframe. Used as dynamic support/resistance; converging AVWAPs from multiple anchors mark especially watched zones.
formula: AVWAP = sum(TypicalPrice_i x Volume_i, from anchor to t) / sum(Volume_i, from anchor to t).
failure_modes: Anchor choice is subjective - different anchors give different lines, inviting confirmation bias; like VWAP it lags increasingly as the anchored window lengthens.
misconceptions: There is no objectively 'correct' anchor - the tool measures the post-event volume-weighted consensus, not a hidden fair value.
example: StockCharts' TSLA example: the session VWAP from the open was skewed by the first 20 minutes, while an AVWAP anchored at the morning low better tracked midday trade.

name: Moving VWAP
definition: A moving average of successive VWAP values over a user-chosen number of periods, producing a volume-weighted average that flows continuously from day to day instead of resetting each session.
intuition: Classic VWAP dies at the close; MVWAP keeps a rolling volume-weighted memory, giving longer-horizon traders a VWAP-like reference across days.
mechanics: Compute intraday VWAP as usual (cumulative typical price x volume over cumulative volume), then average the last n VWAP values; a 10-period MVWAP starts plotting after 10 VWAP points and slides forward, dropping the oldest.
formula: MVWAP(n) = (1/n) x sum of the last n VWAP values, where each VWAP = sum(TypicalPrice x Volume) / sum(Volume) over its calculation window.
failure_modes: Doubly smoothed, it lags more than plain VWAP, and its value depends on how each platform chains daily VWAPs across sessions; there is no single canonical construction.
misconceptions: MVWAP has no end-of-day 'final value' significance the way daily VWAP does - it is a rolling average of averages, not an execution benchmark.
example: If the last five daily VWAP values are 100, 101, 101.5, 102, 102.5, the 5-period MVWAP = 101.4.

name: Volume-weighted moving average
definition: A moving average in which each price is weighted by its bar's volume - bars traded on heavy volume pull the average toward them, so the line tracks where business was actually done rather than treating all bars equally.
intuition: An SMA answers 'average price of the last n bars'; a VWMA answers 'average price weighted by how much traded in each of those bars.'
mechanics: Multiply each close by its volume, sum over n periods, and divide by the sum of volume over n periods. Often compared against an equal-length SMA to judge whether volume-backed prices lead or lag the plain average.
formula: VWMA(n) = sum(C_{t-i} x V_{t-i}, i=0..n-1) / sum(V_{t-i}, i=0..n-1).
failure_modes: A single extreme-volume bar dominates the window, so the average jumps when it enters and again when it leaves; meaningless on instruments without reliable volume such as spot forex.
misconceptions: VWMA is not VWAP: VWAP is cumulative from a session anchor, VWMA is a rolling n-period window - they answer different questions.
example: Tulip Indicators' worked example: closes 81.59-83.61 with volumes around 3.8-7.7M give a first 5-period VWMA of 82.33, versus an equal-weighted SMA of 82.63.

name: Relative volume
definition: The ratio of current trading volume to average volume over a look-back (typically 10-20 sessions), often time-of-day adjusted so that, say, 10:30 a.m. volume is compared with prior 10:30 a.m. volumes; a reading of 1.0 means perfectly normal participation.
intuition: Raw volume is meaningless without context - five million shares is quiet for a mega-cap and extraordinary for a small-cap; RVOL normalizes it.
mechanics: RVOL = current volume / average volume over n sessions; intraday versions divide cumulative volume so far by the average cumulative volume at the same time of day. Traders screen for RVOL of roughly 1.5-2.0 or higher to find 'in play' names.
formula: RVOL = V_current / Average(V, n); time-adjusted form: RVOL(t) = CumV(today, up to t) / Average_n(CumV(up to same time t)).
failure_modes: High RVOL signals attention, not direction - it accompanies both breakouts and dumps; time-of-day effects (open and close volume surges) distort non-adjusted intraday readings.
misconceptions: RVOL is not a buy signal - a spike can mark exhaustion at the end of a move as easily as participation at the start; it measures activity, nothing else.
example: A stock averaging 300,000 shares a day that trades 1,000,000 has RVOL ~ 3.3; TradingSim notes SIGA traded 37M shares versus a ~130k average on its May 2022 news day.

name: Volume oscillator
definition: A MACD-style oscillator applied to volume: the difference between a fast and a slow exponential moving average of volume, usually expressed as a percentage of the slow average (the Percentage Volume Oscillator, defaults 12, 26, 9).
intuition: It shows whether participation is expanding or drying up: positive and rising means short-term volume is running above its longer norm.
mechanics: PVO = (EMA(V,12) - EMA(V,26)) / EMA(V,26) x 100, with a 9-period EMA signal line and a histogram, paralleling the MACD/PPO structure. Used mainly to confirm breakouts - price breaks on rising or positive PVO carry more weight.
formula: PVO = ((EMA(V,12) - EMA(V,26)) / EMA(V,26)) x 100; Signal = EMA(PVO, 9); Histogram = PVO - Signal.
failure_modes: Volume does not trend smoothly, so PVO is choppy and divergences are unreliable; because both EMAs lag, PVO can confirm a breakout only after the fact.
misconceptions: A positive PVO does not say volume is 'high' in any absolute sense - only that the 12-period average exceeds the 26-period; and high volume is neither bullish nor bearish without price context.
example: A 12-day volume EMA of 3.0M against a 26-day EMA of 2.5M gives PVO = +20, matching the surge level StockCharts shows confirming ADM's resistance and support breaks.

name: Chaikin oscillator
definition: Marc Chaikin's momentum-of-money-flow oscillator: the MACD formula applied to the Accumulation/Distribution Line - the 3-day EMA of the ADL minus its 10-day EMA - designed to anticipate turns in accumulation and distribution.
intuition: It is an indicator of an indicator: instead of watching the ADL's slow drift, you watch its momentum cross zero, flagging shifts in buying and selling pressure earlier.
mechanics: Compute the ADL from Money Flow Multiplier times volume; the oscillator = EMA(ADL,3) - EMA(ADL,10). Positive means the ADL is rising (buying pressure), negative means it is falling; divergences with price warn of pressure shifts before zero-line confirmation.
formula: Chaikin Oscillator = EMA(ADL, 3) - EMA(ADL, 10), with ADL the running sum of [((C-L) - (H-C)) / (H-L)] x V.
failure_modes: Three derivations removed from price, it frequently disconnects from it, and the default (3,10) settings cross zero often, producing whipsaws that need confirmation.
misconceptions: A bullish divergence is not yet buying pressure - while the oscillator stays below zero, selling pressure still dominates; confirmation requires a cross into positive territory.
example: If the 3-day EMA of the ADL is 12,000 and the 10-day EMA is 11,000, the oscillator reads +1,000 - the threshold StockCharts uses in its bullish scan.

name: Aroon up
definition: Tushar Chande's 1995 indicator measuring how recently price made a new n-period high, expressed as a 0-100 percentage: 100 when the high occurred in the current period, decaying toward 0 as it recedes into the past.
intuition: Instead of asking how far price moved, Aroon-Up asks how long ago the latest high was - frequent new highs keep it pinned near 100.
mechanics: Aroon-Up = 100 x (n - periods since the n-period high) / n, default n = 25. Readings above 50 mean a new high within the most recent half of the window; sustained 70-100 readings mark strong uptrends.
formula: Aroon-Up(n) = ((n - PeriodsSinceHighestHigh(n)) / n) x 100.
failure_modes: It measures time, not magnitude - a market drifting sideways near its highs keeps Aroon-Up high without real momentum, and the reading decays mechanically as the window ages even when price is flat.
misconceptions: Aroon-Up at 100 does not mean 'overbought, expect reversal' - it only means the latest n-period high happened today.
example: With n = 25 and the 25-day high made 5 days ago: Aroon-Up = (25-5)/25 x 100 = 80.

name: Aroon down
definition: The downside counterpart in Chande's Aroon system: a measure of how recently price made a new n-period low, on a 0-100 scale where 100 means the low was set in the current period.
intuition: It tracks the freshness of new lows; a market printing new lows today has Aroon-Down at 100, and sustained 70-100 readings mark strong downtrends.
mechanics: Aroon-Down = 100 x (n - periods since the n-period low) / n, default 25. Crosses of Aroon-Down above Aroon-Up, moves above 50, and surges to 100 are the three stages of an emerging downtrend signal.
formula: Aroon-Down(n) = ((n - PeriodsSinceLowestLow(n)) / n) x 100.
failure_modes: Same time-not-magnitude limitation as Aroon-Up; both lines can sit low together in consolidations, giving no directional read at all.
misconceptions: A high Aroon-Down is a description of recent lows, not an oversold buy signal.
example: With n = 25 and the 25-day low set 10 days ago: Aroon-Down = (25-10)/25 x 100 = 60.

name: Aroon oscillator
definition: The difference between Aroon-Up and Aroon-Down, compressing Chande's pair into one line bounded between -100 and +100; positive when new highs are more recent than new lows, negative when new lows are more recent.
intuition: It nets the two Aroon lines: +100 means today's bar made a new n-period high while the low is as old as possible; the zero line is the bull-bear divide.
mechanics: Aroon Oscillator = Aroon-Up - Aroon-Down with the same n (default 25). Used for zero-line trend bias and, with +/-50 or +/-90 thresholds, for strong-trend filtering.
formula: AroonOsc(n) = AroonUp(n) - AroonDown(n) = 100 x (PeriodsSinceLowestLow(n) - PeriodsSinceHighestHigh(n)) / n.
failure_modes: It lags because it only reacts once highs and lows age out of the window; choppy markets flip it across zero repeatedly, and it was not designed for classic oscillator divergence signals.
misconceptions: A positive reading does not measure trend strength in price terms - a +40 reading only ranks the recency of highs versus lows.
example: Aroon-Up 80 and Aroon-Down 20 give an oscillator of +60, an upside bias; +100 requires Up = 100 and Down = 0 simultaneously.

name: Chande momentum oscillator
definition: Tushar Chande's momentum oscillator: 100 times the difference between summed up-moves and summed down-moves over n periods divided by their total, bounding raw, unsmoothed momentum between -100 and +100.
intuition: It is a tug-of-war score between up days and down days: if all movement over the window was up, CMO is +100; all down, -100.
mechanics: Sum the gains of up closes and the losses of down closes separately over n periods; CMO = 100 x (Su - Sd)/(Su + Sd). Readings beyond +/-50 are treated as overbought/oversold; divergences and zero-line crosses give trend signals.
formula: CMO(n) = 100 x (Su - Sd) / (Su + Sd), where Su = sum of max(C_i - C_{i-1}, 0) and Sd = sum of max(C_{i-1} - C_i, 0) over n periods.
failure_modes: Unsmoothed, so it is noisier than RSI and reaches its extremes more often; overbought/oversold levels fail in strong trends, as with all bounded oscillators.
misconceptions: CMO is not a smoothed RSI - it nets raw sums rather than Wilder-smoothed average gains and losses, and the +/-50 thresholds are conventions, not validated cutoffs.
example: Over 20 days with up-moves totaling 30 points and down-moves 10: CMO = 100 x (30-10)/(30+10) = +50.

name: Ultimate oscillator
definition: Larry Williams' three-timeframe momentum oscillator (1976; Stocks & Commodities, 1985): a weighted blend (4:2:1) of buying-pressure-to-true-range ratios over 7, 14, and 28 periods, designed to reduce the false divergences of single-timeframe oscillators.
intuition: Short-term momentum dominates the blend but is checked by two longer frames, so a divergence must show weakness across multiple horizons to count.
mechanics: BP = Close - min(Low, prior Close); TR = max(High, prior Close) - min(Low, prior Close); Average_k = sum(BP, k)/sum(TR, k) for k = 7, 14, 28; UO = 100 x (4xAvg7 + 2xAvg14 + Avg28)/7. Williams' buy signal: a bullish divergence whose oscillator low is below 30, confirmed by a break above the divergence high.
formula: UO = 100 x (4 x Avg7 + 2 x Avg14 + 1 x Avg28) / (4+2+1), with Avg_k = sum(BP, k) / sum(TR, k).
failure_modes: The fixed 4:2:1 weighting and divergence-plus-level rules are intricate but still whipsaw; on quiet securities the oscillator may never reach 30 or 70 with default settings, inviting parameter fiddling.
misconceptions: Despite the name it is not 'ultimate' or proven superior - it is one multi-frame weighting scheme among many, and its signals still require confirmation.

name: TRIX
definition: Jack Hutson's momentum oscillator (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, early 1980s): the one-period percentage rate of change of a triple-smoothed exponential moving average (EMA of EMA of EMA), engineered to filter out price moves too small to matter.
intuition: Three rounds of smoothing strip out noise; what remains turning up or down is, in theory, the significant trend cycle.
mechanics: Compute EMA(n) of the close, then EMA(n) of that series, then EMA(n) again (default n = 15); TRIX = 100 x (tripleEMA_t - tripleEMA_{t-1}) / tripleEMA_{t-1}. Traded via signal-line (9-period EMA) crosses, zero-line crosses, and divergences.
formula: EMA1 = EMA(C, n); EMA2 = EMA(EMA1, n); EMA3 = EMA(EMA2, n); TRIX = 100 x (EMA3_t - EMA3_{t-1}) / EMA3_{t-1}.
failure_modes: The triple smoothing lags substantially - StockCharts' Intel example shows three of six signal-line crosses whipsawing in one stretch; in flat markets TRIX hugs zero with ambiguous crosses.
misconceptions: Filtering out 'insignificant' moves also filters the early part of significant ones; TRIX's smoothness is bought with delay, not accuracy.
example: If the triple-smoothed EMA rises from 100.0 to 100.2, TRIX prints +0.2 (percent) for that bar.
